seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Sullivan will sing Guillaume Tell in Italian at the Carlo Felice, Genoa , once on Boxing Night . I have asked him to send you two passes. I hope you will go and hear him. You will not regret it.

closer.add:
not yet come; the tickets aint.
An damifi'm going ennyhow.

div.note: Joyce makes reference to the forthcoming performance of Guillaume Tell on the night of Boxing Day, 26 December. He would have been writing at some point in advance of the performance.

John O’Sullivan, or Sullivan (1877-1955), Irish tenor who was a leading performer of the Paris Opéra and whom JJ was enthusiastically promoting at this time. For a fuller account, see Lucia Joyce to Pound, 22 February 1930, notes.

note.p: On 26 December 1930, John O’Sullivan sang the role of Arnold in the opera Guillaume Tell (1829) by the Italian composer Gioachino Rossini (1792-1868) at the Teatro Carlo Felice, the principal opera house of Genoa, Italy. Arnold, the Swiss hero who with William Tell seeks righteous revenge against the cruel Austrian rulers of their country, was one of the roles with which O’Sullivan was most closely identified. His powerful heroic-tenor voice was suited to the role’s tremendously difficult vocal range, which is severely tested in Act Four by the arias “Asile héréditaire” and “Amis, amis, secondez ma vengeance” (see Lucia Joyce to Pound, 22 February 1930, notes).

Performing with O’Sullivan were the Italian bass Ernesto Dominici (1893-1954); the Italian baritone Benvenuto Franci (1891-1985); the Argentinian spinto soprano Hina Spani (1896-1969); and the Italian bass Enrico Vannuccini (b. 1877). The performance was conducted by Gaetano Bavagnoli (1879-1933), the Italian maestro who was conductor during the Teatro’s winter season. (A list of O’Sullivan’s performances of Arnold in Guillaume Tell is found at http://www.historicaltenors.net/tenorsoperas/arnold/osarnold.html.)

div.note: 26 December, the day after Christmas, is often called Boxing Day in Britain and other countries, possibly for the tradition of giving gifts on that day to servants and the poor.

Pound typed this reply on the reverse of JJ’s letter and evidently sent the page back to JJ. Although Pound wrote his own opera, Le Testament de Villon – an idiosyncratic affair based on rhythmic cadences, much percussion, and the poetry of François Villon (ca. 1431-ca. 1463) – he was not an opera buff. He was deeply interested in medieval music, troubadour songs, and other early developments; and he helped organize many performances of string quartets, sonatas for violin and piano, and other small groups during “Tigullian Musical Seasons” in his adopted town of Rapallo, Italy. With his mistress, the violinist Olga Rudge (1895-1996), Pound helped spur a revival of the music of Antonio Vivaldi (1678-1741). Although Genoa is only twenty miles from Rapallo, the idea that Pound would go there to hear a heroic tenor shows how far JJ’s enthusiasm for O’Sullivan had carried him. (For a fuller account of Le Testament de Villon, see JJ to Pound, 20 March 1926, notes.)
